question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=2\,j$ and $b=3\,i+j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =2\,j+t[(3\,i+j)-2\,j] \\  & =2\,j+t(3\,i-j) \\  & =3t\,i+(2-t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3t$ and $y=2-t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)j \\  & =3\,i-j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t)^{2}-(2-t) \\  & =9{t}^{2}+t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+3\,j)+t[3\,j-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(i+3\,j)-t\,i \\  & =(1-t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1-t$ and $y=3$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)j \\  & =-i \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-t)+3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+j$ and $b=i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+j)+t[(i+2\,j)-(-i+j)] \\  & =(-i+j)+t(2\,i+j) \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t-1$ and $y=t+1$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1+(2t-1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\  & =2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))\cdot \sqrt{5}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-3,1)$ to $(2,3)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-3,1)$ to $(2,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-3\,i+j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-3\,i+j)+t[(2\,i+3\,j)-(-3\,i+j)] \\  & =(-3\,i+j)+t(5\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(5t-3)\,i+(1+2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=5t-3$ and $y=1+2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =5\,i+2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{29}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(5t-3)+(1+2t) \\  & =12t-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12t-5)\cdot \sqrt{29}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{29}{\int }_{0}^{1}(12t-5)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b=-3\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t(b) \\  & =t(-3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-3t\,i+4t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-3t$ and $y=4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =-3\,i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{-3t+4t} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,4)$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,4)$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+4\,j$ and $b=-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+4\,j)+t[(-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j)-(-i+4\,j)] \\  & =(-i+4\,j)+t(-\frac{3}{2}\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)\,i+(4-2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-\frac{3}{2}t-1$ and $y=4-2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-2t)j \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(- \frac{3}{2})^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)+(4-2t) \\  & =-5t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-5t+2)\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-5t+2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,2)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},0)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,2)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},0).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+2\,j$ and $b=\frac{3}{2}\,i.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+2\,j)+t[\frac{3}{2}\,i-(-i+2\,j)] \\  & =(-i+2\,j)+t(\frac{5}{2}\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(\frac{5}{2}t-1)\,i+(-2t+2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=\frac{5}{2}t-1$ and $y=-2t+2$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{5}{2}t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t+2)j \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{5}{2}}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1+(\frac{5}{2}t-1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2t+2) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{5}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-2))\cdot \frac{\sqrt{41}}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{5}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-2))\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(3,- \frac{7}{2})$ to $(-1,- \frac{11}{3})?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,- \frac{7}{2})$ to $(-1,- \frac{11}{3}).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j$ and $b=-i-\frac{11}{3}\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j)+t[(-i-\frac{11}{3}\,j)-(3\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j)] \\  & =(3\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j)+t(-4\,i-\frac{1}{6}\,j) \\  & =(-4t+3)\,i+(-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{6}t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-4t+3$ and $y=-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{6}t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-4t+3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{6}t)j \\  & =-4\,i-\frac{1}{6}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(- \frac{1}{6})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{577}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(-4t+3)^{2}-(-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{6}t) \\  & =16{t}^{2}-\frac{143}{6}t+\frac{25}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(16{t}^{2}-\frac{143}{6}t+\frac{25}{2})\cdot \frac{\sqrt{577}}{6}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{577}}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(16{t}^{2}-\frac{143}{6}t+\frac{25}{2})\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,\frac{13}{3})$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,\frac{13}{3})$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+\frac{13}{3}\,j$ and $b=-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+\frac{13}{3}\,j)+t[(-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j)-(-i+\frac{13}{3}\,j)] \\  & =(-i+\frac{13}{3}\,j)+t(-\frac{3}{2}\,i-\frac{7}{3}\,j) \\  & =(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)\,i+(\frac{13}{3}-\frac{7}{3}t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-\frac{3}{2}t-1$ and $y=\frac{13}{3}-\frac{7}{3}t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{13}{3}-\frac{7}{3}t)j \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,i-\frac{7}{3}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(- \frac{3}{2})^{2}+(- \frac{7}{3})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{277}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)+(\frac{13}{3}-\frac{7}{3}t) \\  & =-\frac{16}{3}t+\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(\frac{7}{2},\frac{13}{3})?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(\frac{7}{2},\frac{13}{3}).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=\frac{7}{2}\,i+\frac{13}{3}\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+3\,j)+t[(\frac{7}{2}\,i+\frac{13}{3}\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(i+3\,j)+t(\frac{5}{2}\,i+\frac{4}{3}\,j) \\  & =(1+\frac{5}{2}t)\,i+(3+\frac{4}{3}t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+\frac{5}{2}t$ and $y=3+\frac{4}{3}t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\frac{5}{2}t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3+\frac{4}{3}t)j \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\,i+\frac{4}{3}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{5}{2}}^{2}+{\frac{4}{3}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{17}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((1+\frac{5}{2}t)+3+\frac{4}{3}t) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4+\frac{23}{6}t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4+\frac{23}{6}t)\cdot \frac{17}{6}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{17}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4+\frac{23}{6}t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-2,- \frac{7}{2})$ to $(1,-1)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-2,- \frac{7}{2})$ to $(1,-1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-2\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j$ and $b=i-j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j)] \\  & =(-2\,i-\frac{7}{2}\,j)+t(3\,i+\frac{5}{2}\,j) \\  & =(3t-2)\,i+(-\frac{7}{2}+\frac{5}{2}t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3t-2$ and $y=-\frac{7}{2}+\frac{5}{2}t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{7}{2}+\frac{5}{2}t)j \\  & =3\,i+\frac{5}{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{\frac{5}{2}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{61}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-2)^{2}-(-\frac{7}{2}+\frac{5}{2}t) \\  & =9{t}^{2}-\frac{29}{2}t+\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-\frac{29}{2}t+\frac{15}{2})\cdot \frac{\sqrt{61}}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{61}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-\frac{29}{2}t+\frac{15}{2})\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,2)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{3})?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,2)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{3}).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+2\,j$ and $b=\frac{3}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+2\,j)+t[(\frac{3}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j)-(-i+2\,j)] \\  & =(-i+2\,j)+t(\frac{5}{2}\,i-\frac{5}{3}\,j) \\  & =(\frac{5}{2}t-1)\,i+(-\frac{5}{3}t+2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=\frac{5}{2}t-1$ and $y=-\frac{5}{3}t+2$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{5}{2}t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{5}{3}t+2)j \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\,i-\frac{5}{3}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{5}{2}}^{2}+(- \frac{5}{3})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1+(\frac{5}{2}t-1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{5}{3}t+2) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5}{3}t-2).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{5}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5}{3}t-2))\cdot \frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{5}{2}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5}{3}t-2))\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t(b) \\  & =t(\frac{3}{2}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}t\,i+t\,j\end{aligned}

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{3}{2}}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{13}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\end{aligned}
